I have an existing React + Vite + JavaScript + Tailwind CSS project called TheCodeHood. It is a directory for finding tech communities and meetups. My GitHub repository is [https://github.com/amelia2802/thecodehood](https://github.com/amelia2802/thecodehood).
I am participating in the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass. I need a small, working feature that I can finish and deploy quickly.
Build: TheCodeHood Community Matchmaker
Add a polished section to my existing website where users can discover ways to connect with tech communities offline.
User experience
Create a card with:
Heading: "Your next connection starts outside."
Short description: "Find your people, step away from the screen, and make something happen in real life."
Interest input: web development, AI, open source, cybersecurity, design, or other.
Location input: city, state, or ZIP code.
Preferred meetup: in-person, online, or either.
Social comfort: "I'm new to meetups", "I'm a little nervous", or "I'm ready to network".
A button labelled "Find my community plan".
After submission, show an AI-generated plan with:
A short, encouraging recommendation.
Two or three practical steps to find and attend a relevant meetup.
One small offline challenge, such as attending a local tech meetup, visiting a coworking event, or talking to one developer.
A simple preparation checklist.
A reminder to verify event details and availability before travelling.
Make the experience welcoming to introverts and beginners. Do not shame people for preferring online communities.
Open-source AI requirements
Use an open-weight language model through Hugging Face Inference Providers. Use the official OpenAI-compatible endpoint:
[https://router.huggingface.co/v1/chat/completions](https://router.huggingface.co/v1/chat/completions)
Select a currently available open-weight model supported by the provider. Verify its model ID and license rather than assuming availability.
Create a small Node.js + Express backend endpoint, for example POST /api/matchmaker. The backend must call the model and return the generated plan.
Security requirements:
Store HF_TOKEN as a server-side environment variable.
Never expose HF_TOKEN or other private credentials in React code, VITE_ variables, Git commits, or browser responses.
Validate and limit user input.
Handle API errors and loading states gracefully.
Do not send unnecessary personal data to the model.
Fit my existing project
Inspect the repository and existing components before changing anything.
Reuse the existing layout, header, footer, styles, and community data where appropriate.
Add a reusable React component and integrate it into the existing page without replacing the whole website.
Match the existing design. Make the new section responsive, accessible, and visually polished.
If the repository already has real community listings, use those as the source of truth. Never invent real organizations, events, addresses, dates, or joining links.
Make it clear that AI suggestions are generated guidance, not verified live event listings.
Deployment
Keep the existing Vite frontend deployable on Render. Provide the backend as a separate Render Web Service if necessary.
Explain the exact build/start commands and required environment variables. Configure CORS to allow only the actual deployed frontend origin. Use the Render-provided PORT value. Update the frontend to call the deployed backend URL through an environment variable such as VITE_API_URL.
Update README.md with the feature, architecture, setup instructions, environment variables, model/provider attribution, deployment links, and remaining limitations.
Testing and delivery
Ensure npm run build succeeds.
Run npm run lint if available and fix relevant issues.
Test input validation, loading, successful responses, and API failures.
Verify that the model token is not present in the frontend bundle.
Do not claim deployment or live testing succeeded unless it actually did.
Show me the files changed and the exact commands and dashboard settings I must use.
Keep the scope small. Do not add authentication, payments, a new database, or unrelated features. Do not replace my existing website. Prioritize a functioning, honest MVP over extra features.
</USER_REQUEST>

# TheCodeHood 🏡

A community directory for developers and technologists to discover local meetups, build connections, and step away from the screen.

Repository: [https://github.com/amelia2802/thecodehood](https://github.com/amelia2802/thecodehood)

---

## 🌿 Hacktoberfest Challenge: Week 1 — Touch Grass

### TheCodeHood Community Matchmaker

As part of the **Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge (Week 1: Touch Grass)**, TheCodeHood introduces the **Community Matchmaker**—an AI-guided feature designed to help developers find practical, comfortable pathways to connect with tech communities in the real world.

### ✨ What It Does
- **Low-Pressure Discovery**: Tailored specifically for introverts, beginners, and seasoned builders alike. Never shames anyone for preferring virtual or self-paced participation.
- **Micro-Goals**: Provides a small, achievable offline challenge (e.g. visiting a local tech meetup, checking out a co-working space, or talking with one developer).
- **Practical Preparation**: Generates concrete steps, preparation checklists (with interactive completion checkboxes), and safety verification reminders.
- **Grounded Source of Truth**: Evaluates verified community listings in the directory as ground truth to prevent hallucinated organizations, fictitious dates, or fake URLs.

---

## 🏗️ Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Vite + React Frontend (Render Static Site)  │
│  - CommunityMatchmaker Form & Card Component │
│  - Calls backend via VITE_API_URL            │
│  - ZERO AI keys or tokens in bundle          │
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │ HTTP POST /api/matchmaker
┌──────────────────────▼───────────────────────┐
│   Node.js + Express Backend (Render Service) │
│   - server/index.js (Port: process.env.PORT) │
│   - CORS restricted to FRONTEND_ORIGIN       │
│   - Input sanitization & bounds checking     │
│   - Grounding against verified communities   │
│   - Server-side HF_TOKEN credential handling │
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │ OpenAI-Compatible Chat Completions
┌──────────────────────▼───────────────────────┐
│   Hugging Face Inference Providers           │
│   https://router.huggingface.co/v1           │
│   Model: meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## 🤖 Open-Source AI Model & Provider Attribution

- **Endpoint**: Official OpenAI-compatible router endpoint:  
  `https://router.huggingface.co/v1/chat/completions`
- **Default Model**: [`meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct)
  - **License**: Llama 3.1 Community License Agreement (open weights, commercial & research use permitted).
- **Alternative Supported Model**: [`Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct)
  - **License**: Apache 2.0 (permissive open source).
- **Attribution**: Powered by Hugging Face Inference Providers. AI outputs are framed transparently as advisory guidance and planning advice rather than verified live tickets.

---

## 🔒 Security & Privacy

1. **Server-Side Token Storage**: `HF_TOKEN` is loaded strictly in the backend via server environment variables. It is **never** prefixed with `VITE_`, never exposed in React code, never bundled into static build artifacts, and never leaked in API responses.
2. **Input Validation**: All client fields (`interest`, `location`, `preferredMeetup`, `socialComfort`) are sanitized, strictly length-limited, and validated before dispatch.
3. **Graceful Degradation**: Handles missing credentials, rate limits (HTTP 429), cold starts (HTTP 503), timeouts, and network disconnects gracefully with clear user guidance.
4. **Minimal Data Surface**: Only generic interest, city/region, and comfort preferences are passed to the model—no names, emails, IP addresses, or tracking identifiers.

---

## 🚀 Local Development Setup

### 1. Prerequisites
- Node.js `v20.x` or higher
- npm `v10.x` or higher

### 2. Installation
```bash
git clone https://github.com/amelia2802/thecodehood.git
cd thecodehood
npm install
```

### 3. Server Configuration
Create a `.env` file in the root directory (or server environment) with your Hugging Face User Access Token:
```env
# Server-side only (Do NOT prefix with VITE_)
HF_TOKEN=hf_your_hugging_face_user_access_token_here
HF_MODEL=meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
PORT=3001
FRONTEND_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
```
*(Get a free token from [https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens](https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens).)*

### 4. Running Locally
Run the backend server:
```bash
npm run server
# Starts backend at http://localhost:3001
```

In a separate terminal, run the Vite frontend:
```bash
npm run dev
# Starts frontend at http://localhost:5173
```
*Note: During local development, Vite proxies `/api` calls directly to `http://localhost:3001`, so no extra frontend configuration is needed.*

### 5. Running Tests & Linting
```bash
# Run Community Matchmaker API automated test suite
npm run test:matchmaker

# Run ESLint
npm run lint

# Verify production build
npm run build
```

---

## 🌐 Deployment on Render

### A. Deploy Backend (Render Web Service)
1. In the **Render Dashboard**, click **New +** > **Web Service**.
2. Connect your GitHub repository: `amelia2802/thecodehood`.
3. Configure the service settings:
   - **Name**: `thecodehood-api`
   - **Environment**: `Node`
   - **Region**: Select closest to your users (e.g., `Oregon (US West)` or `Frankfurt (EU)`)
   - **Branch**: `main`
   - **Build Command**: `npm install`
   - **Start Command**: `npm run server`
4. Add the following **Environment Variables**:
   - `HF_TOKEN`: Your Hugging Face user access token (`hf_...`)
   - `FRONTEND_ORIGIN`: Your deployed frontend URL (e.g. `https://thecodehood.onrender.com`)
   - `HF_MODEL`: `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` (optional, defaults to this model)
   - *Note: Render automatically injects the `PORT` variable.*
5. Click **Create Web Service** and note your deployed service URL (e.g. `https://thecodehood-api.onrender.com`).

### B. Deploy Frontend (Render Static Site)
1. In the **Render Dashboard**, click **New +** > **Static Site**.
2. Connect your GitHub repository: `amelia2802/thecodehood`.
3. Configure the static site settings:
   - **Name**: `thecodehood`
   - **Branch**: `main`
   - **Build Command**: `npm run build`
   - **Publish Directory**: `dist`
4. Add the following **Environment Variable**:
   - `VITE_API_URL`: Your backend URL from Step A (e.g. `https://thecodehood-api.onrender.com`)
5. Click **Create Static Site**.

---

## ⚠️ Remaining Limitations

1. **Cold Start Latency**: Free inference tiers on Hugging Face router endpoints may experience brief cold start latency on first request.
2. **Directory Listings**: Verified listings currently map to verified seed records in `src/data.js`. Future iterations will add automated ingestion of community feeds via RSS/ICS and webhooks.
3. **Safety Verification**: AI guidance provides planning steps and icebreaker suggestions; participants must always verify physical event details, venue safety policies, and codes of conduct directly with organizers before traveling.

---

    "body_markdown": "Ding-dong! The ghouls are gone and the season of Christmas begins; the month long Hacktoberfest wraps up, filled with learning, debugging and late night commits! 🎃 
This year, I learned so much more through contributing to Open Source which I never got from just reading tutorials or doing personal projects. and honestly a big chunk of that credit goes to the Torc community.
_(Before diving into my journey, check out [Torc](https://platform.torc.dev/#/r/ZILxKHb0/cp))_

At the beginning of the month, my feed was full of posts from people on LinkedIn and Twitter buzzing about Hacktoberfest. Everyone seemed so ready and excited. And me? I was like, _"Umm, nice... but where do I even start?"_ My calendar was already packed with other events so I didn't really have time to plan my contributions. 
And that's where the magic of a good tech community kicks in. Around the second week of October, right when Hacktoberfest was in full swing I finally got a break and logged back in. That's when I discovered that Torc discord have a dedicated hacktoberfest channel, shout out to [Jason Torres](https://www.linkedin.com/in/thejasontorres/) for creating the torctoberfest repo. And I got a place to start! My interest was back, but then came the real question: _**what do I contribute to?**_

## The Beginning of torcReads 
While scrolling through the channels I suddenly remembered, I hadn't even read the book we picked for our book club! That's when the idea hit me. Huge thanks to [Angelos Katrantzis](https://www.linkedin.com/in/angeloskatrantzis/) for starting the Torc Book Club; otherwise I might never have thought of this project in the first place! 
The initial plan was simple: build a website to log the books we read each month in the club. But then my brain went _"Wait, why not add more?"_ So I started adding features like study guides and monthly voting options. The frontend came out beautifully; Responsive, Clean and Minimalist. And guess what? My first two PRs got merged! Cool, right? 😎 


![2 PRs Approved](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/xmbvb2uqz3s91gab6la9.png)

After hosting it for testing, I realized something... _Oops it is storing all the data locally!_ Which meant once deployed, everyone would see their own data. Total chaos incoming! 
And here's the twist: I never worked with any backend before. So laptop on, a little googling, some brainstorming with Claude and a few Stack Overflow tabs later; BAM! I discovered Supabase! It lets you store data globally and even offers generous free storage. But of course... I had zero experience integrating a database with frontend.

Still I told myself _"we've got a week and a half before 31st October! Why not learn something new?"_

## My Learnings in the Process

![torcReads Preview](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/qjeaqu2gkbp0gd1cvfsv.png)

While setting up the database with the frontend I learned a few cool things:

- **Row Level Security (RLS)**
Access control that defines who can read, insert, update, or delete specific rows based on policies.

- **Migration Files**
Version controlled SQL scripts that track and apply database schema changes over time, allowing teams to sync database structures across environments.

- **CRUD Operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete)**
The four fundamental database operations: Create adds new data, Read retrieves it, Update modifies it, and Delete removes it.

- **Uploading files to cloud**
Cloud file storage service that uploads files to remote servers and returns public URLs, allowing applications to store and retrieve uploaded content without managing server infrastructure.

- **Organizing files**
Containers that group and organize related files in cloud storage.

- **Public vs Private buckets**
Access control for file storage; public buckets allow anyone with the URL to download files while private buckets require authentication.

Check out the Torctoberfest Repo here: https://github.com/jasonetorres/torctoberfest

Building torcReads taught me far more than just coding. Before this, I thought backend and database were way out of my league. But once hit a real problem, I had no choice but to figure it out! Kudos to [Pat Clark](https://www.linkedin.com/in/pat-clarke-dev/) for reviewing and giving thoughtful feedback on each of my pull requests. 

I realized open source isn't about being an expert in everything and you don't need to know all to get started. It's about showing up, trying things and learning in public. Even a small idea can turn into something valuable when you have a great community guiding you! 

Happy Hacking! 🕸️👻

As developers, we spend hours immersed in code, terminal windows, and debugging sessions. Tech communities thrive online in Discord servers and Slack channels, but something irreplaceable happens when we step away from the keyboard and meet fellow builders face-to-face.

Yet for many beginners, introverts, and developers with social anxiety, showing up to a meetup can feel intimidating: *What if I don't know anyone? What if the talks are over my head? Where do I even begin?*

To solve this, I built **TheCodeHood Community Matchmaker**—an open-source AI guide integrated into [TheCodeHood](https://github.com/amelia2802/thecodehood) that turns the overwhelming prospect of "networking" into gentle, low-pressure micro-goals and grounded real-world action plans.

---

## ✨ What TheCodeHood Community Matchmaker Does

Rather than offering a generic chatbot, the Matchmaker provides structured coaching tailored to the user's energy level:

1. **Low-Pressure Input**: Users share their technical focus (*web development, AI, open source, cybersecurity, design, or other*), location (*city, state, or ZIP*), format preference (*in-person, online, or either*), and social comfort (*"I'm new to meetups", "I'm a little nervous", or "I'm ready to network"*).
2. **Encouraging Recommendations**: Positive, personalized advice that never shames anyone for preferring quiet observation or virtual participation.
3. **Actionable Steps**: 2–3 concrete steps to locate, evaluate, and ease into relevant gatherings.
4. **Touch Grass Micro-Challenge**: An achievable offline goal—such as visiting an open co-working space or talking with just one person about their current project.
5. **Interactive Preparation Checklist**: In-browser toggleable items (charging transit cards, rehearsing a simple 1-sentence intro, setting personal exit boundaries).
6. **Grounded Source of Truth**: Matches against verified directory listings already in the repo, preventing the hallucination of non-existent organizations or addresses.

It doesn't shame you for loving online spaces—instead, it helps bridge the gap smoothly to real-world tech meetups, coworking spaces, and local developer coffee chats.

You can check out the live project repository and explore the code here. _Hosted frontend and backend deployed via Render._

For this challenge, I wanted to leverage open-weight models through the official OpenAI-compatible endpoint provided by Hugging Face Inference Providers `([https://router.huggingface.co/v1/chat/completions](https://router.huggingface.co/v1/chat/completions)`).
